content: At the end of 1998, over 33 million individuals were infected with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), and more than one million children had acquired the infection from their mothers. The objective of this review was to evaluate interventions that could effectively reduce the risk of mother-to-child transmission of HIV, as well as their impact on neonatal and maternal mortality and morbidity. The Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group trials register and the Cochrane Controlled Trials Register were searched to identify relevant studies. Randomized trials were included if they compared any intervention aimed at reducing the risk of mother-to-child transmission of HIV with either a placebo, no treatment, or other interventions. The quality of the trials was assessed, and data were extracted by the reviewer. Zidovudine: Four trials involving 1,585 participants compared zidovudine with placebo. The use of zidovudine was associated with a significant reduction in the risk of mother-to-child transmission of HIV (relative risk [RR] 0.54, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.42–0.69). There was no evidence to suggest that long-course therapy was superior to short-course therapy. Nevirapine: One trial involving 626 women, most of whom breastfed their infants, compared intrapartum and postnatal nevirapine with intrapartum and postnatal zidovudine. Nevirapine significantly reduced the risk of mother-to-child transmission of HIV compared to zidovudine (RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.40–0.83). No trials were available that compared nevirapine with placebo. Caesarean Section: One trial involving 436 participants compared elective caesarean section with anticipated vaginal delivery. Elective caesarean section significantly reduced the risk of mother-to-child transmission of HIV compared to vaginal delivery (RR 0.17, 95% CI 0.05–0.55). Immunoglobulin: One trial involving 501 participants compared hyperimmune immunoglobulin plus zidovudine with non-specific immunoglobulin plus zidovudine. The addition of hyperimmune immunoglobulin to zidovudine did not appear to provide any additional benefit in reducing the risk of mother-to-child transmission (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.29–1.55). Conclusions: Zidovudine, nevirapine, and delivery by elective caesarean section are highly effective interventions for reducing the risk of mother-to-child transmission of HIV.
